description: Solo team from Campinas, working on the challenge Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. Our project, Brasa, calibrates 25 years of NASA FIRMS fire hotspots into one consistent monthly record for Brazil, its 6 biomes and 27 states, and publishes it as an open web calendar with an early-warning view for fire brigades and civil defense. Skills: data analysis, statistics, Python, TypeScript and data visualization. The team is complete.
summary: Brasa turns NASA's two satellite fire records, MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), into one consistent month-by-month calendar of fires for Brazil, its 6 biomes, its 27 states and the Campinas Metro Area. VIIRS sees about 3.8 times more hotspots than MODIS, so simply joining the records makes fire activity appear to triple in 2012 and creates a false rising trend. I calibrated MODIS to VIIRS on 14 years of overlap, validated the result out of sample (R² 0.93), and show estimates with 90% uncertainty intervals. An early-warning panel compares the running total of the current year with every year since 2001. On this record the Pantanal's 2020 disaster, when about 30% of the biome burned, stood out from January, long before its September peak. Replayed on every region and year since 2006, the same signal flagged 16 of the 19 severe fire years before their peak month, a median of 6 months ahead. Firefighters, land managers and researchers can see when and where fire peaks, compare 25 years on equal terms, and download the data.
details:
What it does. The site opens on an animated map of Brazil: every 0.25° cell glows with its fire hotspots, month by month since 2001. Switching it between the raw record and the harmonized one shows the false 2012 jump flare up and vanish, and guided views outline three record fire seasons: the Pantanal in 2020, the Cerrado in 2010 (its worst year, yet only 15th on the raw record) and the state of Amazonas in 2024. Below it, Brasa shows a heatmap of years (2001–2026) by months for any Brazilian state, biome, the whole country or the Campinas Metro Area. Each cell is the number of active-fire hotspots that month on a single, consistent VIIRS-equivalent scale. A side panel reports the peak month, the typical fire season and the long-term trend (Mann-Kendall test with Sen's slope). Users can switch between the harmonized record, a naive splice, MODIS only and VIIRS only, and watch the artificial 2012 jump appear and disappear. A map with a ranked list lets users pick a region, any two regions can be compared side by side (each against its own usual year, so the Campinas Metro Area and São Paulo state share one chart), and every selection downloads as CSV.

Early warning. For the latest year in the selection, Brasa adds up hotspots month by month and draws every earlier year behind it. It says in plain words whether the year is ahead of every earlier year, and since when. It also lists the months that beat the same month in every earlier year. In 2020, about 30% of the Brazilian Pantanal burned (44,998 km², Shimabukuro et al., 2023). On the harmonized record, the Pantanal was ahead of every year from 2001 to 2019 from January on. By the end of June, two months before the usual peak, it had 6.1 times the median hotspots for that point of the year. This comparison is only possible on a harmonized record: on the naive splice, every year since 2012 looks like a record. I then replayed the same check on all 35 regions for every year from 2006 to 2025 (700 region-years), each time using only the years before it. Of the 19 years that ended at 2× or more of their usual total, 16 were ahead of every earlier year before their peak month, a median of 6 months before it; the three misses are Roraima, where the season peaks in the first months of the year. It is a screening signal, not a forecast: a year flagged by the end of July turned severe 41% of the time, against 0.6% for the rest, and the false alarms still ended a median 1.3 times their usual year. A "Where this year stands" list ranks every region by how the current year compares so far. When NASA's yearly archive is not yet out, months of the current year come from the FIRMS API. They are labelled provisional and never used to fit the models.

How it works.

  1. I downloaded 40 yearly NASA FIRMS archives for Brazil (MODIS 2000–2025, VIIRS S-NPP 2012–2025) and kept 28.8 million vegetation-fire detections with nominal or high confidence, plus 1.2 million provisional detections for 2026 from the FIRMS Area API.
  2. Each detection is assigned to a state, a biome and the Campinas Metro Area using IBGE boundaries.
  3. Early MODIS months with only the Terra satellite (before Aqua, mid-2002) are scaled using the Terra-to-(Terra+Aqua) ratio.
  4. On 162 clean months where both sensors overlap, I compared five calibration models with temporal cross-validation and selected a per-region log-log regression with a fire-season term (cross-validated R² 0.93, compared with −0.34 for no harmonization).
  5. 2026 so far (January to October) comes from the FIRMS Area API and is marked as provisional; it is never used to fit the models.
  6. Values before 2012 are back-cast from MODIS with 90% prediction intervals. Months with degraded satellite coverage are flagged, and VIIRS gaps (e.g. August 2022, July 2024) are filled from calibrated MODIS.

Result. Joined naively, Brazil's hotspots jump 3.19× in 2012 and show a false +5.6% per year rising trend (p < 0.001). After harmonization the 2012 step is 0.84×, identical to MODIS alone, and the false rising trend disappears: the harmonized record shows a slight decline instead (−2.1% per year, p = 0.04), in line with MODIS alone (−1.6% per year, not significant).

Benefits. A trustworthy 25-year baseline for fire-season planning, an early-warning signal months before the peak, and honest trend reporting. The model is simple on purpose: I tested five models on years they had not seen, and the most accurate has three parameters per region, so anyone can check it. The record also stays valid after MODIS is retired.

Field check. I asked a public servant who works in public safety in Campinas how the fire season is handled. The city runs a dry-season operation from 1 May to 30 September, set each year by decree (Campinas Decree 24,403/2026), and follows satellite fire alerts during it. Brasa's 25-year record for the Campinas Metro Area matches that window on its own: 71% of hotspots fall between May and September, peaking in August and September. They described 2024 as a heavy year and 2025 and 2026 as calm; in Brasa, 2024 was the region's worst year since 2014, 2025 had 39% fewer hotspots, and 2026 so far is the calmest in the record. The decree also allows the operation to be "brought forward or extended if adverse climate conditions require". That is the decision Brasa is built to inform: real-time alerts show where it is burning now, while Brasa shows whether this year is running ahead of every earlier year. October alone still holds 10% of the region's hotspots, and more than 15% in 2002, 2007 and 2014.

Accessibility. Colour-blind-safe scales, full keyboard navigation of the calendar, a table version of every chart, and responsive design for mobile phones.

Tools. Python (DuckDB, pandas, GeoPandas, statsmodels, pymannkendall), TypeScript, Vite, D3, Observable Plot. Static site on GitHub Pages: no login, no install.

Source code: https://github.com/brasa-br/calendar

Use of AI

I used an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, by Anthropic) to help write the data pipeline, the website and the scripts that record and edit the demo video, and to draft the documentation. I defined the approach, reviewed the code and checked every statistical result against the source data. The demo video is a screen recording of the real website: its captions and overlays were scripted in code, and the satellite image is a NASA Earth Observatory photograph. The project logo is an AI-generated image (Google Gemini), labelled "AI-generated image" on the image itself. The video narration is an AI-generated voice (Kokoro, an open-source text-to-speech model), labelled "Narration: AI-generated voice" on screen for the whole video; it reads the same script as the captions, word for word. No other generative AI images, video or voice are used.
